title: Productionizing LLM Gateways: Architecture, Tradeoffs and Hard Lessons — Kanish Manuja, Twilio
talk_summary: A Twilio principal engineer explains how to productionize an LLM gateway, framing it as a trade-off between availability, latency, guardrails, and cost. He gives concrete mechanisms: per-request cross-provider fallback, per-route timeouts and latency tracking, tail hedging, guardrail placement/timeouts, and decentralized gateways with centralized governance.

takeaways.technique: Per-request cross-provider fallback with cooldown, not blind retries
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of retrying the same slow/expensive LLM call, they try provider A then fall back to provider B in sequence; failing providers are put in cooldown and removed from the request path rather than tripping a global circuit breaker.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Retrying an LLM API eats into your latency budget really fast... blind retries just multiply your cost and your tail latencies.

takeaways.technique: Provision fallback provider with more headroom than primary
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue teams over-test the primary and neglect the fallback; the fallback should have equal or higher capacity/headroom because it is the last line of defense.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your throughputs or your capacity or your headroom should be even higher for the second provider or the fallback provider because that's your last line of defense

takeaways.technique: Per-route, per-model-class timeouts and latency tracking
takeaways.what_they_do: They set timeouts per model class per route and track P99 per model per route rather than a gateway-wide aggregate, because mixed workloads (embeddings vs reasoning) make aggregate numbers meaningless.
takeaways.evidence_quote: set timeouts on per model class per route. That's where that's the number one root cause of your silent outage.

takeaways.what_they_do: For unpredictable reasoning-model latency, fire a second request once the primary has consumed ~P90 of the latency budget to hedge the P99 tail.

takeaways.technique: Guardrail time budget, placement, and fail-open/fail-close choice
takeaways.what_they_do: Guardrails get their own timeout budget so the LLM stays the rate-determining step; they run pre-hook (serial, safe), in parallel (fast, no streaming), or post-hook (audit); and teams explicitly choose fail-open vs fail-close per guardrail.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Your request should never be bound by your guardrail timing. It should always be the LM that is the rate determining step.

takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than one central gateway as a single point of failure, they decentralize traffic handling but centralize governance (cost tracking, rate limits) via plugins/custom code.
